content: Efavirenz levels can be reduced by rifampin due to its effect on hepatic enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised when these drugs are co-administered. Similarly, rifampin decreases the levels or effects of elacestrant and elafibranor by increasing their metabolism through CYP3A4. Alternative drugs should be considered, and close monitoring is recommended. Elagolix levels can be influenced by rifampin through multiple mechanisms, including P-glycoprotein efflux transporter and CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary, and the combined use of elagolix 150 mg daily with rifampin should be limited to six months. Rifampin is contraindicated with elbasvir/grazoprevir due to significant reductions in therapeutic efficacy caused by CYP3A4 induction. Rifampin reduces eletriptan levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating the use of alternative drugs. Eliglustat levels are increased by rifampin through P-glycoprotein inhibition, while rifampin decreases eliglustat levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are required. Eltrombopag levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP1A2 and CYP2C9/10 metabolism, while eltrombopag increases rifampin levels by reducing its metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Rifampin increases eluxadoline levels by decreasing its metabolism, requiring dose adjustments to 75 mg twice daily if co-administered with OATP1B1 inhibitors. Rifampin reduces elvitegravir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, and co-administration with CYP3A inducers is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. Similarly, rifampin decreases the levels of elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir DF, making their co-administration contraindicated. Rifampin reduces enalapril levels by increasing its metabolism, though the clinical significance is unclear. Enasidenib increases rifampin levels, and co-administration with sensitive OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or BCRP substrates should be avoided. If unavoidable, substrate dosages should be reduced, and therapy closely monitored. Encorafenib increases rifampin levels by inhibiting OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 transporters, potentially increasing toxicity. Rifampin decreases encorafenib levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating alternative drugs and close monitoring. Rifampin also reduces enfortumab vedotin levels through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin decreases entrectinib levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, and alternative drugs should be used. Similarly, rifampin reduces enzalutamide levels, and alternative drugs with minimal CYP3A4 induction potential are recommended. If unavoidable, the enzalutamide dose may need to be increased to 240 mg daily, with close monitoring. Eplerenone levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin decreases erdafitinib levels by altering metabolism, while erdafitinib increases rifampin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Alternative drugs are recommended, and administration should be separated by at least six hours if co-administration is unavoidable. Rifampin reduces ergotamine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating alternative drugs. Erlotinib levels are also decreased by rifampin through P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Rifampin reduces erythromycin levels through CYP3A4 metabolism, and alternative drugs should be used. Escitalopram levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Similarly, esomeprazole levels are reduced by rifampin via CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 metabolism, necessitating close monitoring. Estradiol levels are decreased by rifampin through P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs and close monitoring. Rifampin reduces the levels of conjugated synthetic estrogens, esterified estrogens, and estropipate through CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein transport, necessitating alternative drugs and close monitoring. Eszopiclone levels are significantly reduced by rifampin, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Ethanol decreases rifampin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, though the clinical significance is unclear. Rifampin reduces ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Nonhormonal contraceptives are recommended. Ethosuximide levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Rifampin reduces ethotoin levels via CYP2C9/10 metabolism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Etonogestrel levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Etoposide levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein transport, requiring caution and monitoring. Rifampin decreases etrasimod levels via CYP3A4, CYP2C8, and CYP2C9 metabolism, making co-administration contraindicated. Rifampin reduces etravirine levels through CYP2C19, CYP2C9/10, and CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs and close monitoring. Eucalyptus levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Everolimus levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein transport, making co-administration contraindicated. Exemestane levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring dose adjustments to 50 mg daily with meals. Fedratinib levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, and co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inducers is not recommended. Felbamate and felodipine levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Fenfluramine levels are reduced by rifampin, and co-administration with serotonergic drugs may increase the risk of serotonin syndrome. Fentanyl levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially leading to withdrawal symptoms in dependent patients. Therapy modification and close monitoring are required. Fesoterodine levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Fexinidazole levels are increased by rifampin, while rifampin levels are decreased by fexinidazole through CYP2B6 metabolism. Co-administration is not recommended. Fexofenadine levels are reduced by rifampin through P-glycoprotein transport, though the clinical significance is unclear. Finasteride levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Finerenone levels are also reduced by rifampin, necessitating alternative drugs. Flibanserin levels are significantly reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring close monitoring. Rifampin decreases fluconazole levels by increasing its metabolism, while fluconazole reduces rifampin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Close monitoring is recommended. Fludrocortisone levels are reduced by rifampin through P-glycoprotein transport and CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Flurazepam levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Flurbiprofen levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP2C9/10 metabolism, though the clinical significance is unclear. Rifampin increases fluvastatin toxicity while reducing its levels through CYP2C9/10 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Fosamprenavir levels are significantly reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, making co-administration contraindicated. Fosphenytoin levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP2C9/10 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Fostamatinib increases rifampin levels through P-glycoprotein transport, while rifampin reduces fostamatinib levels through CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative drugs are recommended. Fostemsavir levels are significantly reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, making co-administration contraindicated. Frovatriptan levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP1A2 metabolism, though the clinical significance is unclear. Fruquintinib and futibatinib levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Ganaxolone levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, and co-administration with moderate or strong CYP3A4 inducers should be avoided. Gefitinib levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring dose adjustments to 500 mg daily during co-administration. Gentamicin levels are reduced by rifampin through P-glycoprotein transport, necessitating caution and monitoring. Gepirone levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Gilteritinib levels are reduced by rifampin through P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Glasdegib levels are also reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, and co-administration with strong CYP3A inducers should be avoided. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels are significantly reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, making co-administration contraindicated. Glimepiride, glipizide, and glyburide levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP2C9/10 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Guanfacine levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Haloperidol levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating therapy modification and close monitoring. Hydrocodone levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, and caution is required when discontinuing CYP3A4 inducers to avoid potentially fatal respiratory depression. Hydrocortisone levels are decreased by rifampin through P-glycoprotein transport and CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Hydroxyprogesterone caproate levels are reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating alternative drugs. Ibrutinib levels are significantly reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring alternative drugs. Ibuprofen levels are decreased by rifampin through CYP2C9/10 metabolism, though the clinical significance is unclear. Idelalisib levels are significantly reduced by rifampin through CYP3A4 metabolism, making co-administration not recommended. Ifosfamide metabolism is increased by rifampin through CYP2B6 and CYP3A4, potentially increasing toxicity. Close monitoring and caution are required.
